what_its_for: Flumazenil is used to reverse the sleepy or sedated effects of benzodiazepine medicines (such as Valium, Xanax, or Ativan). It is also used to treat overdose from these medicines. It is given in a hospital or clinic setting by a healthcare provider.
how_to_take: Flumazenil is given as an injection directly into your vein (IV) by a doctor or nurse in a medical setting. You will not give this medicine to yourself at home. Your healthcare team will monitor you closely after you receive it.
dosing: Your doctor or nurse will decide the right dose for you based on your situation. The usual starting dose for adults is 0.2 mg given slowly into a vein over 15 seconds. Additional doses may be given every minute if needed, up to a total of 1 mg. For an overdose situation, higher total doses may be used. Children's doses are based on their weight. Your healthcare team will carefully calculate the right amount for you.
missed_dose: Because flumazenil is given in a hospital or clinic by a healthcare professional, you will not need to manage doses on your own. If you have concerns about your treatment schedule, speak with your doctor or nurse.
storage: Flumazenil is stored and handled only by healthcare professionals in a medical setting. It is kept at room temperature (between 59°F and 86°F / 15°C and 30°C) and protected from light. Unused portions of the vial are thrown away after use.
what_to_avoid: After receiving flumazenil, avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or making important decisions for at least 24 hours, or until your doctor says it is safe. Do not drink alcohol or take any sedating medicines, sleeping pills, or anti-anxiety medicines without your doctor's approval. Avoid activities that require you to be fully alert until the effects of the original sedative have fully worn off. Do not leave the medical facility alone — have a responsible adult with you.
when_to_call_doctor: Tell your healthcare provider right away or seek emergency help if you experience: sudden seizures or convulsions, confusion or agitation that gets worse, extreme drowsiness returning after the injection (this can happen because flumazenil wears off faster than the sedative), fast or irregular heartbeat, trouble breathing, chest pain, unusual muscle movements, or feeling like you might pass out. Also tell your doctor if you have a history of seizures, alcohol dependence, or long-term use of benzodiazepines before receiving this medicine.
when_it_works: Flumazenil begins to work very quickly, usually within 1 to 2 minutes after the injection. The effects typically last about 30 to 60 minutes. Because flumazenil wears off faster than most benzodiazepine medicines, sedation may return after the first dose, and you will be monitored closely by your medical team for at least 2 hours or longer.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): May be more sensitive to the effects of flumazenil and will be watched more carefully. Pregnant women: Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits. Flumazenil should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. Breastfeeding mothers: It is not fully known if flumazenil passes into breast milk. Ask your doctor if it is safe to breastfeed after receiving this medicine. Children: Flumazenil can be used in children, but doses are carefully adjusted by weight. Patients with liver disease: The drug may stay in your body longer. Your doctor will adjust the dose or monitoring as needed. Patients with epilepsy or those who take benzodiazepines regularly: Flumazenil may trigger seizures in these patients. Your medical team will take extra precautions.
